decks.title: Life Processes — Part 1: Life processes and nutrition
goals: List the basic life processes and explain why they are needed to maintain life
Describe the events of photosynthesis and the roles of chlorophyll and stomata
Compare autotrophic and different kinds of heterotrophic nutrition
Trace the path of food through the human alimentary canal and state the role of each digestive juice

slides.heading: Life Processes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what keeps living things alive, how green plants make their own food, and how animals, including you, digest food.

visual.alt: Flow: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion together maintain life

slides.narration: Namaste! Even when you are fast asleep, your body is busy. Your heart beats, your lungs breathe, your cells repair themselves and your kidneys clean your blood. All this work needs energy and raw materials, every single moment. The processes that keep this maintenance going are called life processes. In this chapter we study four of them: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. We begin with nutrition, in plants and in humans.

slides.heading: What are life processes?
slides.body_md: Living things are highly organised. Keeping that order needs **energy** and **raw materials** all the time, even at rest. The processes that perform this **maintenance** are the **life processes**.

rows: Takes in food for energy and growth
Breaks down food to release energy
Cell respiration; gas exchange through stomata

visual.alt: Table of the four life processes with what each does and how it happens in humans and plants

slides.narration: How do we decide that something is alive? Growth and movement are clues, but a sleeping dog is still alive even when it does not move. Inside it, molecules are constantly moving as cells repair and rebuild themselves. That maintenance needs energy, which comes from food. So every living thing must take in food, release energy from it, carry materials to every cell and remove wastes. These are the life processes.

slides.heading: Why large organisms need special systems
slides.body_md: In a single-celled organism every part touches the surroundings, so **diffusion** is enough. In a large, multicellular organism most cells are far from the surface, so diffusion is too slow: it needs **specialised organs** for nutrition, breathing, transport and excretion.

nodes.label: Diffusion through the whole surface is enough
Multicellular body, such as a human
Specialised systems: digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory

visual.alt: Flow comparing a single-celled organism, which relies on diffusion, with a multicellular organism, which needs specialised systems

slides.narration: Imagine a tiny village where every house opens onto the main road. Supplies reach every door directly. That is a single-celled organism like Amoeba: oxygen and food simply diffuse in through its surface. Now imagine a huge city like Mumbai, where most homes are far from the highway. It needs trains, buses and pipelines. Large organisms are the same: their cells are deep inside, so they need dedicated systems to bring in food and oxygen and carry away wastes.

slides.body_md: Why can a human not depend on diffusion alone to supply oxygen to all body cells?

slides.heading: Autotrophs and heterotrophs
slides.body_md: **Autotrophs** make their own food from simple inorganic substances (carbon dioxide and water) using sunlight: green plants and some bacteria. **Heterotrophs** depend, directly or indirectly, on food made by autotrophs: animals, fungi and most bacteria.

rows: Made from carbon dioxide and water

visual.alt: Table comparing autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition by food source, energy source, pigment and examples

slides.narration: There are two ways to get food. Autotrophs are self-feeders: a neem tree builds its own food from carbon dioxide, water and sunlight. Heterotrophs must eat food made by others. You are a heterotroph: the rice and dal on your plate were made by plants, and even milk comes from a cow that ate grass. So, in the end, almost every living thing depends on the food that green plants make.

slides.heading: Photosynthesis
slides.body_md: Green plants make **carbohydrates** from **carbon dioxide** and **water** in the presence of **sunlight** and **chlorophyll**, releasing **oxygen**. The carbohydrate is used for energy, and extra is stored as **starch**.

visual.alt: Carbon dioxide and water, with sunlight and chlorophyll, give glucose, oxygen and water

slides.narration: Photosynthesis means putting together with light. Inside the leaf, carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil are combined, using the energy of sunlight captured by chlorophyll, to make glucose. Oxygen is released into the air. Much of the glucose is turned into starch for storage, just as we store extra energy as fat. Every breath of oxygen you take was released by a plant or an alga somewhere.

slides.heading: Three events of photosynthesis
slides.body_md: The process happens in three main steps. They need not follow each other at once: **desert plants** take in carbon dioxide **at night** and store it as an intermediate, which is used in the day.

nodes.label: Light energy becomes chemical energy; water splits into hydrogen and oxygen
Carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrates

visual.alt: Flow of the three events of photosynthesis: absorption of light, conversion to chemical energy with splitting of water, and reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrate

slides.narration: Photosynthesis happens in three steps. First, chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs light. Second, that light energy is converted into chemical energy, and water molecules are split into hydrogen and oxygen; the oxygen escapes. Third, carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrate. In deserts, where opening stomata by day would waste precious water, cactus-like plants take in carbon dioxide at night and use it the next day.

slides.heading: Stomata: tiny pores for gas exchange
slides.body_md: **Stomata** are tiny pores, mostly on the lower surface of leaves. Each is bordered by two **guard cells**. When water flows into the guard cells they swell and the pore **opens**; when they lose water they shrink and the pore **closes**.

slides.narration: Turn a leaf over and look at it under a microscope: you will see thousands of tiny mouths called stomata. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves through them. But open stomata also let water vapour escape. So guard cells act like smart doors. When they are full of water, they swell and bend apart, opening the pore. When the plant is short of water, they go limp and the pore closes, saving water.

slides.heading: Is chlorophyll needed? The variegated leaf test
slides.body_md: A potted plant with **variegated** leaves (green and white patches) is kept in the dark for three days to use up stored starch, then placed in sunlight. A leaf is boiled in alcohol to remove the green colour and tested with **iodine**: only the parts that were **green** turn **blue-black**.

slides.narration: Here is a classic test. Croton and money plant varieties often have leaves with green and white patches. First keep the plant in the dark for three days so that its leaves use up their stored starch. Then put it in sunlight for a day. Boil a leaf in alcohol, carefully in a water bath, to remove the green colour, and add iodine. Only the areas that were green turn blue-black. Starch was made only where chlorophyll was present.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is light needed?
slides.body_md: Neha destarches a potted plant, covers part of one leaf on both sides with a strip of black paper, and keeps the plant in sunlight for six hours. She then tests the leaf for starch. Interpret her results.
bullets: Step 1 — destarching ensures any starch found was made during the experiment.
Step 2 — the uncovered part turns blue-black: starch was made there.
Step 3 — the covered part stays brown: no starch was made.
Step 4 — the only difference between the two parts is light.
Conclusion — **light is necessary for photosynthesis**.

visual.alt: Worked table: the uncovered part of the leaf turned blue-black with iodine while the covered part stayed brown, showing light is needed for photosynthesis

slides.narration: This is how scientists think about experiments. Neha first removed the old starch, so any starch she finds must be new. Then she changed only one thing, light, by covering part of the leaf. The uncovered part made starch; the covered part did not. Because everything else was the same, she can conclude that light is needed. Remember this pattern for exam questions: control, one changed factor, observation and conclusion.

slides.heading: Where do the raw materials come from?
slides.body_md: Besides carbon dioxide and water, plants need **minerals** such as **nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and magnesium** from the soil. Nitrogen is used to make **proteins**; magnesium is part of **chlorophyll**.

rows: Nitrogen (as nitrates or nitrites, or from bacteria)

visual.alt: Table of raw materials for plant nutrition with their source and how they enter the plant

slides.narration: A plant takes carbon dioxide from the air, but everything else comes from the soil. Water and dissolved minerals enter through the roots. Nitrogen is needed to build proteins, and farmers add fertilisers like urea to supply it. Pulse crops such as moong and chana have bacteria in their root nodules that take nitrogen straight from the air. Magnesium sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule.

slides.heading: Heterotrophic nutrition: different strategies
slides.body_md: Heterotrophs obtain food in different ways, depending on the food and the organism.

rows: Break down dead and decaying matter outside the body, then absorb it
Take food from a living host, harming it
Take in whole food and digest it inside the body

visual.alt: Table of saprophytic, parasitic and holozoic nutrition with how food is obtained and examples

slides.narration: Not every heterotroph eats the same way. Bread mould and mushrooms are saprophytes: they release digestive juices onto dead matter and absorb the result. Parasites like ticks on a dog, or the yellow amarbel creeper on a hedge, feed on living hosts. Most animals, including us, are holozoic: we take whole food into our bodies and digest it inside. Each strategy suits its food and its way of life.

slides.heading: How Amoeba feeds
slides.body_md: **Amoeba** pushes out finger-like extensions called **pseudopodia** around a food particle and engulfs it in a **food vacuole**, where it is digested. **Paramoecium** uses hair-like **cilia** to sweep food into a fixed spot, its mouth.

slides.narration: Amoeba has no mouth and no stomach, yet it eats. When it senses a food particle, it pushes out temporary arms called pseudopodia, which flow around the food and trap it in a bubble called a food vacuole. Digestive juices enter the vacuole, and the digested food diffuses into the cytoplasm. Undigested bits are thrown out. Paramoecium, another single-celled creature, has a definite shape and uses beating cilia to sweep food into its mouth.

slides.body_md: Food passes through one long tube, the **alimentary canal**: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus. Glands such as the **salivary glands**, **liver** and **pancreas** pour juices into it.

slides.narration: Your digestive system is a single tube about eight to nine metres long, folded to fit inside you. Food enters at the mouth and travels through the oesophagus, stomach and small intestine, where most digestion and absorption happen, then through the large intestine, before leftovers leave through the anus. Along the way, glands add juices that break large food molecules into small ones the body can absorb. Find each part on the diagram as we go.

slides.heading: From mouth to stomach
slides.body_md: Muscles in the canal push food along by rhythmic contraction: **peristalsis**. A ring of muscle, a **sphincter**, controls the exit of food from the stomach.

rows: Salivary amylase turns starch into sugar
Makes the medium acidic for pepsin; kills germs
Protects the stomach lining from the acid

visual.alt: Table of digestion in the mouth, oesophagus and stomach with secretions and their actions

slides.narration: Chew a piece of roti for a minute and it starts to taste sweet. That is salivary amylase turning starch into sugar. Swallowed food is squeezed down the oesophagus by waves of muscle called peristalsis. In the stomach, gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, the enzyme pepsin and mucus. The acid kills germs and helps pepsin digest proteins, while the mucus protects the stomach wall. Too much acid causes the burning pain called acidity.

slides.heading: Small intestine: digestion is completed
slides.body_md: The **small intestine** is the longest part of the canal. Here **bile** from the liver and **pancreatic juice** from the pancreas act, and the walls release **intestinal juice**, which completes digestion.

nodes.label: Bile (liver, stored in gall bladder): makes the food alkaline and breaks fats into small droplets (emulsification)
Pancreatic juice: trypsin digests proteins; lipase digests emulsified fats
Intestinal juice: final products — glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol

visual.alt: Flow of digestion in the small intestine: bile emulsifies fats and neutralises acid, pancreatic juice digests proteins and fats, intestinal juice completes digestion

slides.narration: Food leaves the stomach acidic, but the enzymes of the small intestine work best in alkaline conditions. Bile from the liver neutralises the acid and breaks fat into tiny droplets, like soap on oily dishes; it has no enzymes. Pancreatic juice brings trypsin for proteins and lipase for fats. Finally, intestinal juice finishes the job: starch becomes glucose, proteins become amino acids, and fats become fatty acids and glycerol.

slides.heading: Absorption through villi
slides.body_md: The inner wall of the small intestine has millions of finger-like **villi** that give a huge surface area. Digested food passes into the **blood capillaries** in each villus (fats into the **lacteal**). The **large intestine** absorbs extra **water**; waste leaves through the anus, controlled by the **anal sphincter**.

slides.narration: Digested food is useful only once it enters the blood. The lining of the small intestine is covered with millions of tiny finger-like villi, which together give a surface many times larger than the skin of your whole body. Each villus is packed with blood capillaries that carry the nutrients to every cell. The large intestine then absorbs most of the remaining water, and the undigested waste is pushed out through the anus.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: following a plate of rice, dal and ghee
slides.body_md: Trace what happens to the starch in rice, the protein in dal and the fat in ghee.
bullets: Step 1 — **starch** (rice): begins in the mouth (salivary amylase), completed in the small intestine → **glucose**.
Step 2 — **protein** (dal): begins in the stomach (pepsin), continues with trypsin, completed by intestinal juice → **amino acids**.
Step 3 — **fat** (ghee): emulsified by bile, digested by lipase → **fatty acids and glycerol**.
Step 4 — all three are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine.
Check — every enzyme turns a large molecule into small, soluble ones.

visual.alt: Worked table tracing starch, protein and fat through digestion with where digestion begins, enzymes and end products

slides.narration: Let us follow a simple plate of rice, dal and ghee. The rice is mostly starch; its digestion begins in your mouth and ends in the small intestine as glucose. The protein in dal is first attacked in the stomach by pepsin, then by trypsin, and ends as amino acids. The ghee waits until the small intestine, where bile breaks it into droplets and lipase digests it. All the end products are absorbed through the villi.

slides.heading: Quick check: where is food absorbed?
slides.body_md: In which part of the alimentary canal is most digested food absorbed into the blood?
slides.narration: Final check for this part. Think about the finger-like villi and the organ whose wall carries them. Choose your answer.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Life processes — nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion — maintain life; large organisms need special systems because diffusion is too slow.
Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll; it releases oxygen; stomata control gas exchange.
Heterotrophs: saprophytic, parasitic or holozoic; Amoeba uses pseudopodia and a food vacuole.
Human digestion: saliva (starch), stomach (acid, pepsin, mucus), small intestine (bile, pancreatic and intestinal juices), absorption by villi, water absorbed in the large intestine.

visual.alt: Summary table of the main event in each part of the human alimentary canal

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 1. Life processes keep living things organised, and large organisms need special systems for them. Green plants make food by photosynthesis, using carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll, and they control gas exchange through stomata. Heterotrophs get food in different ways. In humans, digestion starts in the mouth, continues in the stomach, finishes in the small intestine, and the villi absorb the products.

slides.heading: Exam tips: nutrition
bullets: Photosynthesis equation: write sunlight and chlorophyll on the arrow; the products are glucose, oxygen (and water).
Stomata open when guard cells **take in water and swell**; close when they lose water.
Starch-test answers: mention **destarching**, **boiling in alcohol**, the **iodine** colour (blue-black) and the conclusion.
Bile has **no enzymes**: it emulsifies fats and makes the medium alkaline.
Name the enzyme **and** its substrate and product: salivary amylase, starch → sugar; pepsin and trypsin, proteins; lipase, fats.
Alimentary canal diagram: label at least mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small and large intestine, anus.
slides.narration: Here is how to score full marks. In the photosynthesis equation, put sunlight and chlorophyll on the arrow. Explain stomata in terms of guard cells gaining or losing water. In experiments, mention destarching, boiling the leaf in alcohol, the iodine colour and the conclusion. Remember that bile has no enzymes. Always name an enzyme together with what it acts on and what it makes. And practise drawing the alimentary canal with neat, labelled lines.

decks.title: Life Processes — Part 2: Respiration and transport in human beings
goals: Compare aerobic and anaerobic breakdown of glucose in yeast, muscle and mitochondria
Describe the human respiratory system and gas exchange in the alveoli
Describe the structure of the human heart and double circulation
Explain the roles of blood, lymph, blood vessels and platelets

slides.heading: Respiration and transportation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how cells **release energy** from food, how we **breathe**, and how the **heart and blood** carry oxygen and food to every cell.

visual.alt: Glucose and oxygen give carbon dioxide and water in aerobic respiration, releasing energy
visual.caption: Energy is released and stored as ATP.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. The food you digested is still locked-up energy. To run, think or even blink, your cells must release that energy, and that process is respiration. It needs oxygen, which your lungs take from the air, and a delivery system to carry oxygen and food to billions of cells: your heart and blood. Let us follow the energy from glucose to your muscles.

slides.heading: Breaking down glucose: three pathways
slides.body_md: Respiration always begins in the **cytoplasm**, where glucose (6 carbons) is broken into **pyruvate** (3 carbons). What happens next depends on whether **oxygen** is available.

nodes.label: No oxygen, in yeast: ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy
Lack of oxygen, in muscle cells: lactic acid + energy
Oxygen present, in mitochondria: carbon dioxide + water + much energy

visual.alt: Flow: glucose is broken into pyruvate in the cytoplasm; pyruvate then gives ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast, lactic acid in oxygen-starved muscle, or carbon dioxide and water in mitochondria

slides.narration: Every cell starts the same way: in the cytoplasm, one glucose molecule with six carbon atoms is split into two pyruvate molecules with three carbons each, releasing a little energy. Then the paths divide. Yeast without oxygen turns pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Your muscles, when short of oxygen, make lactic acid. With enough oxygen, mitochondria break pyruvate down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing far more energy.

slides.heading: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration
slides.body_md: **Aerobic** respiration uses oxygen and releases **much more energy**. **Anaerobic** respiration happens without oxygen and releases **less energy**.

rows: Ethanol and carbon dioxide (yeast); lactic acid (muscle)

visual.alt: Table comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration by oxygen need, location, products, energy released and examples

slides.narration: Here is the comparison you must know. Aerobic respiration needs oxygen, takes place partly in the mitochondria, gives carbon dioxide and water, and releases a lot of energy. Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen, only in the cytoplasm, and gives far less energy. Yeast uses it to make ethanol and carbon dioxide, and your muscles switch to it for short bursts, making lactic acid.

slides.heading: ATP: the energy currency
slides.body_md: Energy released in respiration is used to make **ATP**. When a cell needs energy, ATP is broken down, releasing energy for **muscle contraction**, **making proteins**, **conducting nerve impulses** and other work.

nodes.label: ATP broken down: energy for muscles, nerves, building proteins

visual.alt: Flow: respiration of glucose makes ATP, which is broken down to release energy for cell activities

slides.narration: Cells cannot use the energy of glucose directly, just as you cannot pay a shopkeeper with a gold bar. First, respiration changes it into small, convenient coins called ATP. Whenever a muscle needs to contract or a nerve needs to send a message, ATP is spent, releasing its stored energy. That is why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: idli batter and a sprinter
slides.body_md: Explain (a) why idli batter rises overnight and (b) why a sprinter feels cramps after a 400 m race.
bullets: Step 1 — (a) yeast and bacteria in the batter respire **anaerobically**.
Step 2 — they break down sugars, releasing **carbon dioxide**, which forms bubbles and makes the batter rise.
Step 3 — (b) during the sprint, muscles need energy faster than oxygen can arrive.
Step 4 — muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration and **lactic acid** builds up, causing cramps.
Check — both happen without enough oxygen; the products differ (carbon dioxide vs lactic acid).

visual.alt: Worked table comparing fermentation in idli batter, which releases carbon dioxide, with muscle cramps, caused by lactic acid

slides.narration: Two everyday puzzles, one idea. Overnight, microbes in idli batter break down sugars without oxygen and release carbon dioxide, which puffs the batter up. In a sprinter's leg, muscles burn energy faster than the blood can bring oxygen, so they switch to anaerobic respiration and lactic acid accumulates, causing cramps. Rest and deep breathing bring in oxygen and clear the lactic acid. The key in both cases is a lack of oxygen.

slides.body_md: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the three pathways from pyruvate. Which one belongs to yeast? Pick the option that names both products.

slides.heading: Gas exchange in plants and water animals
slides.body_md: Plants exchange gases by **diffusion** through **stomata**, stem openings and root surfaces. Aquatic animals use **oxygen dissolved in water**, which is much less than in air, so they **breathe faster**.

rows: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, so overall oxygen is released
Only respiration: carbon dioxide is released
Dissolved oxygen is low, so breathing is fast

visual.alt: Table of gas exchange in plants by day and night, fish and land animals

slides.narration: Plants respire all the time, day and night. In daylight, though, photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide faster than respiration makes it, so overall plants give out oxygen. At night, with no photosynthesis, they release carbon dioxide. Fish face a different problem: water holds far less oxygen than air. That is why a fish in a pond opens and closes its gills so rapidly, pumping water over them all the time.

slides.heading: The human respiratory system
slides.body_md: Air enters through the **nostrils**, where **hairs and mucus** filter it, then passes through the **pharynx**, **larynx** and **trachea** (kept open by **rings of cartilage**) into the **bronchi**, **bronchioles** and finally the **alveoli** in the **lungs**.

slides.narration: Trace the path of a breath. Air enters your nose, where tiny hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and germs. It passes the throat and the voice box, then goes down the windpipe, or trachea. Rings of cartilage keep the trachea open so it never collapses. The trachea splits into two bronchi, one for each lung, which branch again and again into fine bronchioles. Each ends in clusters of tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli.

slides.heading: Breathing in and out
slides.body_md: When we breathe in, the **ribs lift** and the **diaphragm flattens**, so the chest cavity becomes larger and air is sucked into the lungs. Breathing out reverses this. The lungs always keep some air (**residual volume**), so there is time for gas exchange.

rows: Is pushed out of the lungs

visual.alt: Table comparing the movements of ribs, diaphragm and chest cavity during breathing in and breathing out

slides.narration: Put your hands on your ribs and breathe in deeply. You can feel them rise and move outwards, while the diaphragm, a sheet of muscle below the lungs, flattens. The chest cavity gets bigger, pressure inside drops, and air rushes in. Breathe out, and the ribs fall while the diaphragm domes up again, squeezing air out. Even after the deepest breath out, some air remains in the lungs, so oxygen exchange never stops.

slides.heading: Gas exchange in the alveoli
slides.body_md: The alveoli give a very large surface with very thin walls and a rich supply of **blood capillaries**. **Oxygen** diffuses into the blood and is carried by **haemoglobin** in red blood cells; **carbon dioxide**, mostly dissolved in the blood, diffuses out.

slides.narration: The alveoli are where the real exchange happens. Their walls are only one cell thick and wrapped in a net of blood capillaries. Oxygen from the air diffuses into the blood, where haemoglobin in red blood cells picks it up. Carbon dioxide, carried mostly dissolved in the blood plasma, diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out. Spread flat, the alveoli would cover an area of about eighty square metres.

slides.body_md: Why do the lungs contain millions of tiny alveoli instead of a few large air sacs?

slides.heading: Blood: a fluid connective tissue
slides.body_md: Blood consists of a fluid, **plasma**, in which **cells** are suspended. It carries food, oxygen, carbon dioxide, wastes and hormones.

rows: Carries food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form; carries salts and hormones
Help blood to clot at a wound, stopping blood loss

visual.alt: Table of the components of blood and the job of each

slides.narration: Blood is a liquid tissue. The straw-coloured plasma carries dissolved food, carbon dioxide, wastes and hormones. Red blood cells, full of haemoglobin, carry oxygen; that is why a lack of iron, needed for haemoglobin, makes people tired and pale, a condition called anaemia. White blood cells fight germs. Platelets rush to a cut and help form a clot, so that we do not keep bleeding from a small scratch.

slides.heading: The human heart
slides.body_md: The heart is a muscular pump with **four chambers**: two **atria** that receive blood and two **ventricles** that pump it out. The **right side** handles **deoxygenated** blood and the **left side** **oxygenated** blood. **Valves** prevent backflow.

visual.caption: Seen from the front, so the right side of the heart is on your left. Blue: deoxygenated blood; red: oxygenated blood.

slides.narration: Your heart is about the size of your fist and beats around seventy times a minute, all your life. Its upper chambers, the atria, collect blood; its lower chambers, the ventricles, pump it out. The right side receives used, deoxygenated blood from the body and sends it to the lungs. The left side receives fresh, oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the whole body. Valves act like one-way doors.

slides.heading: Double circulation
slides.body_md: Blood passes through the heart **twice** in each complete circuit: once on the way to the lungs (**pulmonary circulation**) and once on the way to the body (**systemic circulation**).

visual.alt: Flow of double circulation: body to right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle and back to the body

slides.narration: Follow one drop of blood. It returns from the body through the vena cava into the right atrium, then drops into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. There it picks up oxygen and returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aorta to the whole body. Twice through the heart in one round trip: double circulation.

slides.heading: Why four chambers?
slides.body_md: Keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood **separate** gives the body a very efficient oxygen supply. Birds and mammals need this because they use a lot of energy to **keep their body temperature constant**.

rows: Single: blood passes through the heart once per circuit
Some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood

visual.alt: Table comparing the number of heart chambers and type of circulation in fish, amphibians and reptiles, and birds and mammals

slides.narration: Why does a sparrow or a human need such an elaborate heart? Birds and mammals keep their bodies warm all the time, which burns a lot of energy and needs a rich oxygen supply. A four-chambered heart never lets used blood mix with fresh blood. Frogs and lizards, whose body temperature follows the surroundings, manage with three chambers and some mixing. Fish have just two chambers: their blood is oxygenated in the gills and goes straight on to the body.

slides.heading: Quick check: the pumping chamber
slides.body_md: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to all parts of the body?
slides.narration: Quick check. Decide which side of the heart carries oxygenated blood, and whether atria or ventricles do the pumping. Then choose.

slides.heading: Arteries, veins and capillaries
slides.body_md: **Arteries** carry blood **away** from the heart under high pressure, so their walls are **thick and elastic**. **Veins** bring blood **back** to the heart; their walls are thinner and they have **valves**. **Capillaries**, with walls **one cell thick**, link the two and allow exchange with cells.

slides.narration: Blood travels in three kinds of tubes. Arteries leave the heart; each heartbeat sends a surge of high pressure through them, so they have thick, stretchy walls. You feel that surge as your pulse at the wrist. Veins return blood at low pressure; they have thinner walls and valves that stop blood flowing backwards. In between, tiny capillaries, with walls just one cell thick, let food and oxygen pass into cells and wastes pass out.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much blood does the heart pump?
slides.body_md: Riya's pulse rate is **72 beats per minute**, and each beat of her left ventricle pumps about **70 mL** of blood. How much blood does it pump in one minute, in litres?
bullets: Step 1 — volume per minute = beats per minute × volume per beat.
Step 2 — $72 \times 70 = 5040$ mL.
Step 3 — convert: $5040 \div 1000 = 5.04$ L per minute.
Check — an adult has about 5 litres of blood, so the whole volume passes through the heart roughly once every minute.

visual.alt: Worked table: 72 beats per minute times 70 mL per beat gives 5040 mL, or 5.04 litres, of blood pumped per minute

slides.narration: Let us put numbers on the heart's work. Riya's heart beats seventy two times a minute, and each beat sends about seventy millilitres of blood into the aorta. Multiply: five thousand and forty millilitres, or just over five litres, every minute. That is about the total amount of blood in an adult's body. So, roughly, all your blood passes through your heart once a minute, every minute of your life.

slides.heading: Blood pressure
slides.body_md: **Blood pressure** is the force blood exerts on the walls of vessels. It is higher in arteries. It is measured with a **sphygmomanometer** and written as **systolic/diastolic**, normally about **120/80 mm of mercury**.

rows: Caused by narrowing (constriction) of arterioles; can burst vessels and cause internal bleeding

visual.alt: Table of systolic and diastolic blood pressure with normal values, and the cause and danger of high blood pressure

slides.narration: At a health camp, a nurse wraps a cuff around your arm and reads two numbers, such as one hundred and twenty over eighty. The first, systolic pressure, is measured when the ventricles squeeze. The second, diastolic, is measured when they relax. Narrowing of small arteries raises the pressure, a condition called hypertension. It can burst blood vessels, so doctors advise less salt, regular exercise and check-ups.

slides.heading: Lymph: the second transport fluid
slides.body_md: Some plasma, proteins and blood cells escape through capillary walls into the spaces between cells as **tissue fluid**. This drains into **lymphatic capillaries** as **lymph**, which carries **digested fat** from the intestine and returns **excess fluid** to the blood.

visual.alt: Flow: fluid leaks from blood capillaries into tissues, drains into lymphatic vessels as lymph, and returns to the blood in large veins

slides.narration: Blood does not travel alone. As it squeezes through capillaries, some liquid leaks into the spaces around cells, bathing them. This tissue fluid is collected by a second set of thin vessels and is then called lymph. Lymph is colourless and has fewer proteins than plasma. It carries fats absorbed in the villi of the intestine, and it returns the extra fluid to the bloodstream. Without it, our tissues would swell up.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Glucose → pyruvate in the cytoplasm; then ethanol + carbon dioxide (yeast), lactic acid (muscle) or carbon dioxide + water in mitochondria (aerobic, most energy). Energy is stored as ATP.
Air path: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli; gas exchange by diffusion; haemoglobin carries oxygen.
Heart: four chambers, right side deoxygenated, left side oxygenated; valves; double circulation.
Arteries (thick walls), veins (valves), capillaries (one cell thick); platelets clot blood; lymph carries fats and returns fluid.

rows: Thickest wall: pumps to whole body

visual.alt: Summary table of key structures in respiration and circulation with their main feature

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 2. Cells release energy from glucose by respiration, aerobic or anaerobic, and store it as ATP. We breathe air into millions of alveoli, where oxygen enters the blood. The four-chambered heart keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart and pumps it in a double circulation. Arteries, veins and capillaries carry it, platelets seal wounds, and lymph returns leaked fluid and carries fats.

slides.heading: Exam tips: respiration and transport
bullets: Write the three pathways with **where** they happen (cytoplasm, mitochondria) and the **products**.
Cramps = **lactic acid**; yeast = **ethanol + carbon dioxide**.

Remember the exception: the **pulmonary artery** carries deoxygenated blood and the **pulmonary veins** carry oxygenated blood.

Lymph: give two functions — carrying digested fat and draining excess tissue fluid.

slides.heading: Transport in plants and excretion
slides.body_md: Part 3 — how water climbs to the top of a tall tree, how food travels around a plant, and how kidneys clean our blood.

visual.alt: Flow of water through a plant: from soil to root hairs, up the xylem to the leaves, and out into the air as water vapour

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 3. A coconut palm on a Kerala beach lifts water from the sand to leaves twenty metres up, without a single pump. Meanwhile, the sugar made in its leaves must reach the roots and the growing coconuts. And in your body, two fist-sized kidneys quietly filter all your blood many times a day. Let us see how plants move materials, and how living things get rid of their wastes.

slides.heading: Two transport tissues in plants
slides.body_md: Plants have two conducting tissues. **Xylem** carries **water and minerals** from the roots upwards. **Phloem** carries **food** made in the leaves to all parts. Plants need less energy than animals, so their transport systems can be slower.

rows: Food (mainly sucrose), amino acids and other substances
Up or down, to wherever it is needed

visual.alt: Table comparing xylem and phloem by what they carry, direction, driving force and cells

slides.narration: A plant has two sets of pipes running side by side. Xylem is the water main: it carries water and minerals from the roots up to the leaves. Phloem is the food delivery service: it carries sugars from the leaves to roots, fruits, seeds and growing buds. Because plants do not run or jump, they need far less energy than animals, so these systems can work slowly and steadily.

slides.heading: Water up, food everywhere
slides.body_md: Water and minerals enter the **root hairs** and rise through **xylem**. **Phloem** carries food from the leaves to storage organs and growing parts. Water is lost from the leaves as vapour: **transpiration**.

slides.narration: Follow the blue arrow first. Root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil, and these move up the xylem through the stem into the leaves. Some of that water is used in photosynthesis, but most evaporates through the stomata. Now follow the green arrow: phloem carries the food made in the leaves to the roots, stems, fruits and seeds. In a sugarcane field, phloem is busy filling the stems with sugar.

slides.heading: How water rises: root pressure and transpiration pull
slides.body_md: Root cells take up **ions** from the soil, so water moves into the root and is pushed upwards: **root pressure**, important **at night**. In the **day**, evaporation of water from leaves creates a **suction** that pulls water up the xylem: **transpiration pull**, the main force.

rows: Ions taken up by root cells; water follows into the xylem
Water evaporates from leaf cells through stomata
In the day, when stomata are open

visual.alt: Table comparing root pressure, which pushes water up from below at night, with transpiration pull, which pulls water up from above during the day

slides.narration: Two forces lift water. At the bottom, root cells actively take in mineral ions, so water flows into the root and builds up a gentle push called root pressure. It matters most at night. In daylight, the stomata are open and water evaporates from the leaves. Each molecule that leaves pulls the next one up behind it, like beads on a string. This transpiration pull is far stronger and lifts water to the top of tall trees.

slides.heading: Quick check: the main force
slides.body_md: What is the main force that moves water up the xylem of a tall tree during the day?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about when stomata are open and what is happening at the leaf surface then. Choose the force that acts from above.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: do leaves cause water loss?
slides.body_md: Vikram takes two similar potted plants, removes all the leaves from plant B, wraps both pots in plastic so that the soil cannot lose water, and weighs them before and after six hours in sunlight. Interpret the results.
bullets: Step 1 — plastic on the pots means any mass lost must come from the plant parts above the soil.
Step 2 — plant A (with leaves) lost 36 g; plant B (no leaves) lost 4 g.
Step 3 — the difference, $36 - 4 = 32$ g, is due to the leaves.
Step 4 — conclusion: most water is lost through the **leaves**, by **transpiration** through stomata.
Check — plant B still lost a little water, through the stem surface.

visual.alt: Worked table: the plant with leaves lost 36 g of water in six hours while the plant without leaves lost 4 g, so most water loss is through the leaves

slides.narration: Vikram's experiment is a fair test. Wrapping the pots stops water evaporating from the soil, so only the plant can lose water. The leafy plant lost thirty six grams in six hours, the leafless one only four. The thirty two gram difference was lost through the leaves, mostly through stomata. That is transpiration. It is why farmers in hot weather water crops in the evening, and why newly planted saplings are often trimmed of extra leaves.

slides.heading: Why transpiration matters
slides.body_md: Transpiration helps in the **absorption and upward movement of water and minerals** and in **cooling** the plant, much like sweating cools us.

nodes.label: Water and minerals rise from the roots

visual.alt: Flow: evaporation from leaves creates suction that lifts water and minerals, and also cools the leaves

slides.narration: Transpiration is not just a loss. The steady evaporation from leaves keeps water and minerals flowing up from the roots, delivering nutrients without any pump. It also cools the leaves on a hot afternoon, just as sweat cools your skin. That is why the shade of a neem tree feels cooler than the shade of a tin roof: the tree is constantly evaporating water.

slides.heading: Translocation: moving food in phloem
slides.body_md: The movement of food in phloem is **translocation**. It carries **sucrose**, amino acids and other substances, and it **uses energy from ATP**. Sugar loaded into phloem draws in water, and the pressure pushes the food to where it is needed.

nodes.label: Sucrose loaded into phloem using ATP
Food moves to roots, fruits, seeds, buds

visual.alt: Flow of translocation: sugar made in leaves is loaded into phloem using ATP, water enters and the pressure moves food to roots, fruits, seeds and buds

slides.narration: Phloem works differently from xylem. Sugar made in the leaves is actively loaded into phloem, using energy from ATP. This draws water in, raising the pressure, which pushes the food along to where the pressure is lower, such as roots, fruits or growing buds. The direction can change with the plant's needs: in spring, sugar stored in roots and stems is sent up to the opening buds.

slides.heading: Excretion in humans: the urinary system
slides.body_md: **Excretion** removes harmful nitrogenous wastes, such as **urea**, from the body. The human excretory system has two **kidneys**, two **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and the **urethra**.

slides.narration: When cells break down proteins, they produce nitrogen-containing wastes like urea, which would poison the body if they built up. The kidneys, two bean-shaped organs at the back of your abdomen, filter these wastes out of the blood. Urine trickles down two tubes called ureters into the urinary bladder, a muscular bag that stores it. It leaves the body through the urethra. We control the bladder through nerves, which is why we can wait until we reach a toilet.

visual.caption: Schematic, not to scale. Each kidney contains about a million nephrons.

slides.narration: Each kidney contains about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons. At the start of each one is a cup, Bowman's capsule, wrapped around a tight knot of blood capillaries, the glomerulus. Blood is filtered here. The filtered liquid then flows along a long, looped tubule, which is wrapped in more capillaries. Finally, the liquid that remains, now urine, drains into a collecting duct and on to the ureter.

slides.heading: How urine is formed
slides.body_md: **Filtration**: in the glomerulus, water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea pass from the blood into Bowman's capsule. **Selective reabsorption**: in the tubule, useful substances and much of the water return to the blood. The rest is **urine**.

nodes.label: Filtration into Bowman’s capsule: water, glucose, amino acids, salts, urea
Tubule: glucose, amino acids, salts and much water reabsorbed into the blood
Urine (water, urea, salts) to collecting duct, ureter and bladder

visual.alt: Flow of urine formation: filtration in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption in the tubule, and urine collected and passed to the bladder

slides.narration: Urine is made in two main steps. First, filtration: blood pressure in the glomerulus pushes water and small molecules, both useful ones like glucose and harmful ones like urea, into Bowman's capsule. Second, selective reabsorption: as this filtrate flows along the tubule, the glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water are taken back into the blood. How much water is reabsorbed depends on how much extra water the body has. What remains is urine.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much filtrate is reabsorbed?
slides.body_md: An adult's kidneys form about **180 L** of filtrate a day, but only about **1.5 L** of urine is passed. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
bullets: Step 1 — volume reabsorbed = $180 - 1.5 = 178.5$ L.
Step 2 — percentage = $\dfrac{178.5}{180} \times 100 \approx 99.2$ %.
Step 3 — so less than 1 % of the filtrate leaves as urine.
Check — this explains why urine is concentrated in wastes even though filtration is so large.

visual.alt: Worked table: of about 180 litres of filtrate a day, about 178.5 litres, nearly 99.2 percent, is reabsorbed and about 1.5 litres leaves as urine

slides.narration: The numbers are astonishing. Your kidneys filter about one hundred and eighty litres of fluid every day, enough to fill nine large buckets. Yet you pass only about one and a half litres of urine. Subtract, then divide by one hundred and eighty: over ninety nine percent of the filtrate is taken back into the blood. The kidney is not a simple sieve; it is a careful recycler that keeps what the body needs.

slides.heading: Artificial kidney: haemodialysis
slides.body_md: When kidneys fail, an **artificial kidney** cleans the blood. Blood flows through long tubes with **semi-permeable** linings, bathed in **dialysing fluid** that has the same osmotic pressure as blood but **no nitrogenous wastes**. Wastes diffuse out, and the cleaned blood returns to the body. Unlike the kidney, there is **no reabsorption**.

Urea and other wastes diffuse into the fluid
Cleaned blood returned to a vein

visual.alt: Flow of haemodialysis: blood from an artery passes through a dialyser where wastes diffuse into dialysing fluid, and the cleaned blood is returned to a vein

slides.narration: If both kidneys stop working, wastes build up in the blood and the person can die. Haemodialysis saves lives. Blood is led out of the body through a machine, past thin semi-permeable tubes bathed in a specially made fluid. Urea and other wastes diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, and the cleaned blood is returned. Patients often need this two or three times a week, or a kidney transplant from a donor.

slides.heading: How plants get rid of wastes
slides.body_md: Plants have no special excretory organs; they use several strategies.

rows: Oxygen (from photosynthesis), carbon dioxide, water vapour
Wastes stored in vacuoles of cells
Stored in old xylem, which no longer conducts water
Released into the soil around the roots

visual.alt: Table of ways in which plants get rid of wastes: through stomata, falling leaves, cell vacuoles, gums and resins in old xylem, and into the soil

slides.narration: Plants handle waste quietly. Extra oxygen and water vapour leave through the stomata. Many wastes are parked in vacuoles or in leaves that will soon fall, so a tree shedding its leaves in autumn is also throwing out its rubbish. Old, non-working xylem fills with gums and resins; the gum on a babool tree and the resin on a pine are examples. Some wastes are simply released into the surrounding soil.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 3
bullets: Xylem carries water and minerals upwards (root pressure at night, transpiration pull by day); phloem carries food both ways using ATP (translocation).
Transpiration helps water and mineral movement and cools the plant.
Urinary system: kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra; the nephron is the functional unit.
Urine formation: filtration in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption in the tubule; dialysis cleans blood when kidneys fail, without reabsorption.
Plants remove wastes through stomata, falling leaves, vacuoles, gums and resins, and into the soil.

visual.alt: Summary table of transport and excretion processes with where they happen and a key point for each

slides.narration: Let us wrap up the chapter. In plants, xylem lifts water using root pressure and transpiration pull, while phloem moves food wherever it is needed, using energy. In humans, kidneys filter the blood in a million nephrons and reabsorb almost everything useful, leaving urine. Dialysis can stand in for failed kidneys. And plants dispose of their wastes in clever, quiet ways. Read the table aloud once more.

slides.heading: Exam tips: transport in plants and excretion
bullets: Xylem vs phloem: give **what**, **direction** and **force** — a three-point comparison earns full marks.
Say **transpiration pull** for day and **root pressure** for night.
Nephron diagram: label glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, tubule, collecting duct and blood vessels.
Urine formation = **filtration + selective reabsorption**; name what is reabsorbed.
Dialysis: semi-permeable tubes, dialysing fluid without wastes, **no reabsorption**.
Plant excretion: list at least three methods.
slides.narration: Here is how to score full marks. Compare xylem and phloem on three points: what they carry, which direction and what drives them. Match transpiration pull with daytime and root pressure with night. Learn the nephron labels. Describe urine formation as filtration followed by selective reabsorption, naming glucose, amino acids, salts and water. For dialysis, mention semi-permeable tubes and the missing reabsorption. And list three ways plants remove wastes.

notes.title: Life Processes — Notes

sections.heading: 1. What are life processes?
sections.body_md:
Living organisms are highly organised; keeping this order (**maintenance**) needs energy and raw materials all the time, even at rest. **Molecular movement** inside cells is a basic sign of life.

The basic **life processes** are **nutrition**, **respiration**, **transportation** and **excretion**.

In single-celled organisms the whole surface is in contact with the surroundings, so **diffusion** is enough. In large multicellular organisms most cells are far from the surface, so diffusion is too slow and specialised tissues and organ systems are needed.

key_terms.definition_md: Processes that together perform the maintenance job: nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion.
Taking in food (an energy source) and using it for energy and growth.
Breaking down food in cells to release energy.
Removal of harmful metabolic wastes from the body.

visual.alt: Four life processes contributing to the maintenance of life

sections.heading: 2. Autotrophic nutrition and photosynthesis
sections.body_md:
**Autotrophs** (green plants, some bacteria) make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll — **photosynthesis**. Excess carbohydrate is stored as **starch**.

**Events of photosynthesis:** (i) absorption of light energy by **chlorophyll**; (ii) conversion of light energy to chemical energy and **splitting of water** into hydrogen and oxygen; (iii) **reduction of carbon dioxide** to carbohydrates. Desert plants take in carbon dioxide at night and use it during the day.

**Stomata** are tiny pores, mostly on the lower surface of leaves, for exchange of gases. **Guard cells** swell with water and open the pore; when they lose water the pore closes, reducing water loss.

**Raw materials:** carbon dioxide from air (through stomata); water and minerals (nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, magnesium) from soil through roots. Nitrogen is used to make proteins.

**Experiments:** a variegated leaf shows that **chlorophyll** is necessary (starch only in green parts); a plant with potassium hydroxide in a closed jar shows that **carbon dioxide** is necessary; covering part of a leaf shows that **light** is necessary. Plants are **destarched** in the dark first; leaves are boiled in alcohol to remove chlorophyll before the iodine test.

key_terms.definition_md: An organism that makes its own food from simple inorganic substances.
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy.
Tiny pores in the leaf epidermis, each bordered by two guard cells, for gas exchange.

sections.heading: 3. Heterotrophic nutrition and human digestion
sections.body_md:
**Heterotrophs** depend on food made by others: **saprophytic** (fungi such as bread mould, mushrooms, yeast), **parasitic** (Cuscuta, ticks, lice, tapeworm), **holozoic** (Amoeba, humans). **Amoeba** engulfs food with **pseudopodia** into a **food vacuole**; **Paramoecium** uses **cilia**.

**Human alimentary canal:** mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus. Food is moved by **peristalsis**.
- **Mouth:** teeth chew; tongue mixes; **salivary amylase** converts starch into sugar.
- **Stomach:** gastric glands release **hydrochloric acid** (acidic medium, kills germs), **pepsin** (proteins) and **mucus** (protects the lining). A **sphincter** controls exit of food.
- **Small intestine** (longest part): **bile** from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) makes the food alkaline and **emulsifies fats**; **pancreatic juice** has **trypsin** (proteins) and **lipase** (emulsified fats); **intestinal juice** completes digestion — proteins → amino acids, carbohydrates → glucose, fats → fatty acids and glycerol. **Villi** greatly increase the surface for **absorption** into blood.
- **Large intestine:** absorbs water; the **anal sphincter** controls removal of waste.
Herbivores have a longer small intestine than carnivores, to digest cellulose.

key_terms.definition_md: Rhythmic contraction of muscles of the alimentary canal that pushes food forward.
Breaking large fat globules into small droplets (by bile), so that lipase can act faster.
Finger-like projections of the inner wall of the small intestine that increase the surface area for absorption.
A ring of muscle that controls an opening, such as the exit from the stomach or the anus.

sections.heading: 4. Respiration
sections.body_md:
In the **cytoplasm**, glucose (6-carbon) is broken into **pyruvate** (3-carbon) with a little energy. Then:
- **Without oxygen (yeast):** pyruvate → **ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy** (fermentation).
- **Lack of oxygen (muscle cells):** pyruvate → **lactic acid + energy** (causes cramps).
- **With oxygen (mitochondria):** pyruvate → **carbon dioxide + water + much energy** (aerobic).
Energy is stored as **ATP**, the energy currency of the cell, and used for muscle contraction, protein synthesis and nerve impulses.

**Plants** exchange gases by diffusion through stomata, stem openings and roots; by day photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide so net oxygen is released; at night carbon dioxide is released. **Aquatic animals** breathe faster because dissolved oxygen is low.

**Human respiratory system:** nostrils (hairs, mucus filter air) → pharynx → larynx → **trachea** (rings of cartilage stop it collapsing) → **bronchi** → **bronchioles** → **alveoli**. Breathing in: ribs lift and diaphragm flattens, enlarging the chest cavity. Alveoli give a large surface (about 80 m²) with thin walls and many capillaries; oxygen is carried by **haemoglobin** in red blood cells; carbon dioxide mostly dissolved in blood. **Residual volume** of air remains in the lungs.

key_terms.definition_md: Breakdown of glucose using oxygen, giving carbon dioxide, water and much energy.
Breakdown of glucose without oxygen, giving less energy (ethanol and carbon dioxide, or lactic acid).
Adenosine triphosphate, the energy currency of the cell.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.

nodes.label: Yeast, no oxygen: ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy

Mitochondria, oxygen: carbon dioxide + water + energy

sections.heading: 5. Transportation in human beings
sections.body_md:
**Blood**: plasma (carries food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form), red blood cells (haemoglobin carries oxygen), white blood cells, and **platelets** (clot blood at wounds).

**Heart**: four chambers. The **right atrium** receives deoxygenated blood from the body (vena cava) → **right ventricle** → **pulmonary artery** → lungs → **pulmonary veins** → **left atrium** → **left ventricle** (thickest wall) → **aorta** → body. **Valves** prevent backflow. Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: **double circulation**. Separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood gives an efficient oxygen supply, needed by birds and mammals, which maintain a constant body temperature. Fish have 2 chambers; amphibians and many reptiles 3.

**Blood vessels**: **arteries** (thick, elastic walls; carry blood away from the heart), **veins** (thinner walls, valves; carry blood to the heart), **capillaries** (walls one cell thick; exchange with cells).

**Blood pressure**: normal about 120/80 mm of mercury (systolic/diastolic), measured with a sphygmomanometer; high blood pressure (hypertension) is caused by constriction of arterioles and can rupture vessels.

**Lymph**: tissue fluid that drains into lymphatic vessels; carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid back into the blood.

key_terms.definition_md: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit of the body.
Blood cells that help blood to clot at the site of an injury.
Colourless fluid formed from tissue fluid; carries fats and returns excess fluid to the blood.
Pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract (about 120 mm of mercury).

sections.heading: 6. Transportation in plants
sections.body_md:
**Xylem** carries water and minerals from roots to leaves. Root cells take up ions, so water enters the root and is pushed up (**root pressure**, important at night). In the day, evaporation of water from leaves (**transpiration**) creates a suction (**transpiration pull**), the main force moving water up. Transpiration also helps absorption of minerals and **regulates temperature**.

**Phloem** carries food (sucrose), amino acids and other substances — **translocation** — in any direction, to roots, fruits, seeds and growing parts. It uses energy from **ATP**: sugar loaded into phloem draws in water, and the pressure moves the material.

key_terms.definition_md: Loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata.
Transport of soluble products of photosynthesis through phloem.
Pressure in the root that pushes water up the xylem, important at night.

sections.heading: 7. Excretion in human beings and plants
sections.body_md:
**Human excretory system:** a pair of **kidneys**, **ureters**, **urinary bladder** and **urethra**. Each kidney has about a million **nephrons**: a **glomerulus** (cluster of capillaries) inside **Bowman's capsule**, then a long **tubule** that drains into a **collecting duct**.
- **Filtration** in the glomerulus: water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea pass into the capsule.
- **Selective reabsorption** in the tubule: glucose, amino acids, salts and much water return to the blood (about 180 L of filtrate a day gives only 1–2 L of urine).
- Urine is stored in the bladder and released through the urethra (under nervous control).

**Haemodialysis (artificial kidney):** blood passes through long semi-permeable tubes in a dialysing fluid with the same osmotic pressure as blood but no nitrogenous wastes; wastes diffuse out; there is **no reabsorption**.

**Plants:** oxygen and water vapour leave through stomata; wastes stored in leaves are lost when leaves fall; wastes stored in vacuoles; **gums and resins** stored in old xylem; some wastes released into the soil.

key_terms.definition_md: The basic filtering unit of the kidney.
A cluster of blood capillaries inside Bowman’s capsule where blood is filtered.

Removal of nitrogenous wastes from blood by an artificial kidney using diffusion through a semi-permeable membrane.
